contributions.headingText: Leiomyoma is a benign tumour of smooth muscle.

8890/0 Leiomyoma, NOS

8897/1 Smooth muscle tumour of uncertain malignant potential
2E86.1 Leiomyoma of other or unspecified sites
Leiomyomas can be found in all organs of the urinary tract, most frequently in the urinary bladder.

Most bladder and urethral tumours are detected incidentally during cystoscopy or imaging, but some may present with obstruction, irritative voiding symptoms, and/or haemorrhage. Kidney leiomyomas are more commonly an incidental finding. Penile and scrotal leiomyomas manifest as palpable masses.

Leiomyomas most commonly occur in the urinary bladder and urethra {9215185; 11859200}, with a wide age range but predominantly in middle-aged adults, and with a female predominance. The scrotum is another common site {24832157; 1879812}. Renal leiomyomas are rare, and many reported cases represent angiomyolipoma {25517956}. When carefully diagnosed, renal leiomyomas have a striking female predominance and are usually located in the renal hilum associated with blood vessels. Leiomyoma is the second most common mesenchymal neoplasm of the paratestis, after lipoma, with a predilection for the epididymis {22832642; 28459169}. Rare penile leiomyomas have been described {11880097}, but some reported cases represent penile myointimoma. Although prostatic leiomyomas have been described, their distinction from prostatic stromal hyperplasia and neoplasia is subjective {18774494}. Rare tumours in immunocompromised patients have been associated with EBV {16112056}.

Most leiomyomas are small (mean size: 20 mm), but tumours as large as 250 mm have been reported {8116123}. Tumours are well circumscribed and tan to white with a bulging, whorled cut surface.

Neoplastic cells closely resemble normal smooth muscle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei. They are arranged in orderly intersecting fascicles. They have little or no nuclear atypia, and they have at most an extremely low level of mitotic activity. Rare examples of leiomyoma with bizarre nuclei have been described in the scrotum, paratestis, and urinary bladder, but long-term follow-up data are limited {11517827; 24832157; 20154594}.

Tumour cells are positive for SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon, at least focally, but negative for S100. In the kidney, negative staining for cathepsin K is useful to distinguish leiomyoma from angiomyolipoma {25517956}. ER and PR expression is common in renal and urethral leiomyomas {15242374; 25517956}.
Essential: intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.

Leiomyomas are treated by biopsy and surveillance, transurethral enucleation/resection, or segmental resection (for large tumours). Resection is curative; recurrence is probably due to incomplete excision {20154594}.
